[0] everyday_reading (E): Everyday reading: as in poetry or Python, line breaks and indentation carry meaning. Java rule: the compiler treats all whitespace between tokens as equivalent; layout is for human readers only (some spaces separate words, e.g. public class).
[1] misconception (M) -> WhitespaceIsSignificant: wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers consider all whitespace in program text (outside quotation marks) to be equivalent; layout is for human readers.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> WhitespaceIsSignificant: Applies the 'layout is ignored' rule unevenly: follows the braces on one trace but the indentation on another, e.g. treats a mis-indented line after a braceless if as part of the branch. (here mixing in: "Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line")

[0] names_the_element (N): Program layout is the use of whitespace (one statement per line, indentation one level per nested block) to make program structure visible; it is a style convention, not syntax.
[1] states_the_rule (S): Whitespace is needed only to separate adjacent words; otherwise all whitespace is equivalent, so the whole HelloWorld program can be written on one line; by convention, indent consistently to show nesting.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): Layout has no execution order of its own: execution follows statements and braces, regardless of lines and indentation.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Changing layout produces the same program output; only whitespace inside string literals appears in the output.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): Re-formatting changes no state and no behaviour; it only changes how readable the text is.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): Indentation should show which statements belong to which block; braces, not indentation, decide it, so wrong indentation misleads.
[1] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Purpose: make the program's structure (or intended structure) apparent so it is easier to read and to find errors.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> WhitespaceIsSignificant: Re-indenting or re-wrapping lines (outside string literals) keeps behaviour; removing a needed space between words (publicclass) breaks compilation.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Always use consistent indentation and one statement per line (an editor can auto-format); it matters most in nested code, and checking indentation helps spot syntax errors.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Indentation does not create a block. Kind: silent logic error. Trigger class: a second statement indented under a braceless if or while, expected to be conditional or repeated
[3] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: Some spaces are required between words. Kind: compile-time. Trigger class: keywords run together, e.g. publicclassGoodbye

wrong: Indents nested blocks inconsistently, so the visual nesting differs from the real nesting. | right: Indent consistently, one level deeper for each nested block, so the layout shows the real nesting; the compiler ignores indentation.
